current_episode.title: Ep.183 -Bringing Structure and Systems to Accidental CEOs

guest.bio_context: Val Coyne began her career in hospitality, managing a family restaurant in Italy and later a chain of restaurants, bistros, bars and bakeries in the Noosa region on Australia's Sunshine Coast. She transitioned into technology as a founding member of a startup building software for the disability sector, where she learned to build systems in growing companies. She subsequently exited that business to launch her current consultancy, now working with C-suite executives, CEOs and COOs to align technology, people and process.

context.real_quote: Technology always, always, always comes last. Typically, first comes process, second comes people, and third comes technology.
key_stats: 27 steps: example number of process steps Val uses to illustrate over-complicated operations before transformation
30, 40, 50 different pieces of software: typical number of unintegrated software platforms accumulated by growing businesses without proactive planning
3, 5, 6 years: time period during which software may gain 10 additional features unknown to users who purchased it
Two annual rhythms: Val recommends one annual full audit and one quarterly smaller check of software inventory and usage

pending_qa.q: What is the responsibility framework for managing technology redundancy and software audits in growing organizations?
pending_qa.r: It is not one person's fault—it's part of business growth. However, organizations should create an explicit organizational chart with clear roles, responsibilities and accountabilities. The responsibility typically sits with a finance manager or operations manager who has a pulse on all departments. Additionally, conduct an annual stock-take audit of all software, licenses, costs and usage, and a quarterly check to review whether new features or changes have occurred.

pending_qa.q: What are the common challenges that accidental CEOs face when scaling their businesses?
pending_qa.r: Accidental CEOs—often high-performing specialists or founders—typically exhibit lack of clarity, structure and follow-through. They show resistance to systems, structure and guardrails that scaling requires, and may sabotage transformation efforts without even realizing it. When promoted operations managers or COOs face similar blocks: they continue wearing multiple hats from their previous roles instead of stepping fully into their new leadership identity.

pending_qa.q: What first step should leadership take to support an accidental CEO or newly promoted operations manager in their transformation?
pending_qa.r: Slow down and bring together the leadership team to decide on an organizational chart together. Explicitly define which seats exist, what responsibilities and accountabilities come with each seat, and decide who should sit in each seat based on skills, mindset and capacity.
